articles.title: Quad Steps Up Regional Cooperation Across the Indo-Pacific in 2026
articles.text:
The Quad’s engagements in 2026 reflected a more substantive approach and a greater clarity on its role in the Indo-Pacific. Through three separate foreign ministers’ meetings in New Delhi, Manila and Atlanta, the grouping has sharpened its common priorities, translated commitments into concrete action and expanded its engagement, a report has stated.
It noted that the Quad foreign ministers held their third meeting of the year last week on the margins of the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Atlanta, following their earlier engagements in New Delhi in May and Manila in July.
Despite these regular interactions, attention has largely remained focused on the long-delayed Quad Leaders’ Summit, which is expected to be held in Manila later this month, a report in online magazine ‘The Diplomat’ highlighted.
“The summit has been the focus of much debate since the 2025 Quad Leaders’ summit, which was scheduled to be hosted by New Delhi, fell through. The leaders’ convening is understandably much awaited since it would be the first since U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to the White House. Moreover, it could put to rest some of the ever-growing speculation on the Quad’s future amid cascading geopolitical conflicts, energy and tech supply constraints, and conjecture over an emergent G3 model (China, Russia, and the U.S.) of managing “spheres of influence,” the report mentioned.
“However, even without a leaders’ summit, 2026 has been significant for the Quad. Three foreign minister-level convenings resulted in the finalization of joint priorities, announcements being put into action, and the broadening of engagement touch-points,” it added.
The report noted that the year 2026 has brought greater clarity to the Quad’s role in the Indo-Pacific. Alongside its clearer position against “economic coercion”, the grouping’s decision to describe its members as “ASEAN Comprehensive Strategic Partners” marks an important development.
“In July 2026, at their meeting in Manila, the Quad nations declared their support for the “practical implementation of the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific (AOIP)” through shared priorities of maritime and transnational security, economic prosperity and security, critical and emerging technologies, and humanitarian assistance and emergency response,” it stated.
The joint statement issued after the Quad meeting in Atlanta also provided updates on several emerging initiatives discussed during the May 2026 meeting in New Delhi. These included the second “Quad-at-Sea” Ship Observer mission, held in September 2026, and the second Indo-Pacific Logistics Network (IPLN) Tabletop Exercise (TTX), hosted by Japan’s Ministry of Defence during the same month, The Diplomat mentioned.
(IANS)

articles.title: IAF Identifies Four Key Technology Priorities for Indigenous Drones
articles.text:
Indigenous propulsion, autonomous software, resilient navigation and standardised interfaces emerged as four key technology priorities at the Indian Air Force’s Outreach Programme.
On 21 October, the Indian Air Force held a stakeholder session at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi, to share its Unmanned and Autonomous Systems Roadmap with industry.
The roadmap describes a layered, networked family of unmanned systems that are reliable, resilient and built to work alongside existing and future manned aircraft. Its stated aim is to give industry a clearer view of future operational needs, so that research, development and manufacturing can line up with them.
The session also made one point plainly: self-reliance in unmanned systems is an operational need, not only an aspiration. Four technology areas were named as needing focused work to reduce dependence on outside sources – indigenous propulsion, autonomous software, resilient navigation and standardised interfaces.
These aren’t only defence problems. Any drone that carries heavy loads over rivers, hills or power lines depends on the same things: propulsion that stays reliable under load, navigation that holds up when conditions are poor, software that behaves predictably, and interfaces that work across systems and suppliers.
The drone industry in India is being pushed to build more of its core technology at home, and that will shape what is possible in power, infrastructure and logistics as well.

articles.title: Euronaval 2026: France Orders 32-Cell Aster Missile Upgrade for FDI Frigates
articles.text:
The French Directorate General of Armaments (DGA) has officially finalized an order with Naval Group and MBDA to double the air defense capabilities of the French Navy’s Defense and Intervention Frigates (FDI), increasing their capacity from 16 to 32 Aster missiles.

At the Euronaval 2026 exhibition in Paris, the French Ministry of Armed Forces announced the formalization of a contract that will significantly upgrade the firepower of the Marine Nationale’s newest frigates.

This official contract award locks in the industrial execution of a capability enhancement that was previously debated in parliament. As Naval News reported in November 2025, the French National Assembly’s Defense Commission confirmed during the 2026 budget discussions that the final two FDI frigates would be built with 32 cells and the first three vessels—starting with the lead ship Amiral Ronarc’h—would subsequently undergo retrofits.

According to the French Ministry of Armed Forces, the upgrade aims to bolster the lethality and resilience of the FDI frigates in an increasingly demanding operational environment. The ministry noted that this effort reflects France’s commitment to continuously adapting its naval capabilities to evolving strategic threats, ensuring the frigates are fully equipped for high-intensity maritime conflicts and saturation attacks.

The FDI program, managed by the DGA, is a central pillar of the French Navy’s modernization strategy. These 4,500-ton, data-centric, multi-mission warships are designed to operate in all types of sea states and threat environments. The lead ship of the class, Amiral Ronarc’h, was delivered to the French Navy in October 2025, marking the beginning of a five-ship fleet for the Marine Nationale.

The Aster missile family remains the backbone of European naval air defense, currently equipping the aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle, Horizon-class air defense destroyers, FREMM multi-mission frigates, and the new FDIs.

  • Aster 15: With a range of over 30 kilometers, this variant specializes in intercepting aircraft and sea-skimming anti-ship missiles.
  • Aster 30: Extends the fleet’s defensive umbrella beyond 120 kilometers and, in its most advanced variants, integrates some anti-ballistic missile capabilities.

Both missiles feature exceptionally high maneuverability thanks to the unique “PIF-PAF” control system and lateral thrusters fitted in the Aster missile, allowing them to reliably intercept highly agile modern airborne threats.

The move to a 32-cell vertical launch system (VLS) configuration also perfectly aligns the French Navy’s frigates with the platform’s successful export variants. The FDI has already proven to be an export success for Naval Group, most notably with the Hellenic Navy and the Royal Swedish Navy. Greece’s Kimon-class frigates were ordered from the outset with the expanded 32-missile configuration, highlighting the international demand for deep magazines and sustained air defense capabilities. Sweden similarly signed a contract in August 2026 for four FDI frigates to form its future Luleå-class. This export momentum continues, with Naval Group actively running ongoing campaigns to pitch the FDI for future frigate programs in Denmark and Belgium.

During Euronaval 2026, Naval Group unvealed the “FDI family”, which now includes a new, larger and more powerful variant alongside the existing FDI in its various configurations. The larger FDI, sporting a 9-meter-long section added amidships, is mainly intended for export, according to a DGA source who spoke to Naval News.

articles.title: India’s Three-Tier Naval Air Defence Plan Explained
articles.text:
The modern anti-ship threat comes in layers, so the defence against it must also come in layers. A sea-skimming cruise missile that pops up over the horizon provides a ship’s crew with a few seconds to react, but a swarm of drones can saturate a single launcher. An anti-ship ballistic missile diving at Mach 7 from the edge of space threaten the fleet’s most valued hulls. No single missile can answer all three.
The Indian Navy’s answer is a tiered air-defence architecture for its frontline warships, built around three families of vertically launched surface-to-air missiles: an indigenous short-range layer, the battle-proven medium-range Barak-8, and the newest and most ambitious 250 km interceptor derived from DRDO’s Project Kusha will also be able to tackle anti-ship ballistic missiles.
The innermost tier is the Vertical Launch Short-Range Surface-to-Air Missile (or VL-SRSAM) is the first indigenously developed shipborne SAM system to enter service and is a surface-launched variant of the Astra Mk-1 air-to-air missile. It will replace the Israeli Barak-1 point-defence system that has guarded Indian warships since the early 2000s but whose roughly 12 km range and vulnerability to electronic countermeasures have become liabilities against modern saturation attacks.
VL-SRSAM is canister-launched vertically, a cold-launch arrangement that ejects the missile before its motor ignites reducing the thermal signature, allowing dense salvos from compact launchers and giving 360-degree coverage without the ship having to manoeuvre. It carries an indigenous radio-frequency seeker for all-weather performance. Published range figures vary across a band: DRDO has quoted up to 80 km but other accounts place the practical engagement envelope nearer 40-50 km. Either way it is a clear step up from Barak-1.
The missile pairs with a new four-panel X-band AESA multi-function radar with a detection range of over 200 km, whose developmental trials were completed in 2024 and is now in production at a defence public-sector unit. Bharat Electronics Limited won an order worth about ₹850 crore from Cochin Shipyard in September 2024 to supply six sets for the Next Generation Missile Vessels. A March 2025 test showed the missile’s near-boundary low-altitude capability against a high-speed sea-skimming target to be particularly relevant in close-in defence.
Induction is expected from around 2030, beginning with the Project 15A/B destroyers and extending to the Kamorta-class corvettes, the Next Generation Missile Vessels, the Next Generation Corvettes and the Brahmaputra-class frigates. Full integration across 20-25 major combatants is targeted by roughly 2035.
The middle layer: MR-SAM (Barak-8)
The middle tier is the Medium-Range SAM, the naval version of the Indo-Israel Barak-8 jointly developed by DRDO and Israel Aerospace Industries and integrated in India by Bharat Electronics Limited. The naval variant is commonly known as LR-SAM; the land-based configuration is called MR-SAM. It engages targets from as close as 500 metres to about 70 km, with a speed of around Mach 2; an extended-range version is said to reach up to 150 km.
The range is defined by the Multifunctional Surveillance and Threat Alert Radar (MF-STAR), an active phased-array radar with a surveillance range of about 350 km, able to track over a thousand air targets simultaneously and control the fire of a weapon control system and vertical launchers. The Barak-8 is already the standard area-defence weapon on the Navy’s most capable surface combatants, the Kolkata-class and Visakhapatnam-class destroyers, the carrier INS Vikrant, the Nilgiri-class (Project 17A) frigates and the Kamorta-class corvettes. In 2019 the Navy demonstrated cooperative engagement capability (one ship controlling another’s missiles against separate targets at extended range), and in January 2025 India signed a further contract with Bharat Dynamics for over 70 MRSAM rounds, valued at about ₹2,960 crore, to arm future warships.
The outer layer: a Kusha-based interceptor
The outermost tier is in the drawing board and test phase, a long-range interceptor drawn from Project Kusha DRDO’s indigenous ‘Desi S-400’ family, formally the Extended Range Air Defence System. Project Kusha comprises three interceptors M1 (about 150 km), M2 (about 250 km), and M3 (350-400 km) sharing a common kill vehicle and guidance pack but using progressively larger boosters. The M1 has its maiden flight test on 23 July 2026; trials of M2 and M3 are planned for 2027 and 2028, with induction from around 2030.
For the Navy, the relevant round is the M2-derived naval variant, reported to have a range of 200-300 km and, critically, the ability to intercept anti-ship ballistic missiles travelling at up to Mach 7. That gives the naval variant a dual capability akin to the US Navy’s SM-6: engaging aircraft and cruise missiles at long range, and providing a lower-tier ballistic-missile defence for the fleet to complement the dedicated naval ballistic-missile-defence system tested in 2023.
The Navy intends a scalable deployment rather than a one-size-fits-all approach: the shorter-range M1 on smaller surface combatants, and the longer-legged M2 on its largest destroyers and (in future) aircraft carriers the air-defence command nodes of a carrier strike group. Given the common kill-vehicle and guidance, the same missile family can be fitted to different classes (with common logistic, maintenance and training), but the larger booster requires deeper and heavier vertical launch modules, hence M2 is reserved for the biggest hulls. A new, much larger radar spanning about six metres, roughly four times the array on the Visakhapatnam class is being developed for the Next Generation Destroyer to support the extended envelope.
Together the three levels represent an evolutionary progression in the intensity of the threat they are intended to handle. VL-SRSAM responds to threats that have neared the battle group and must be destroyed at close range, such as sea-skimming missiles and aircraft within a range of several tens of kilometers. The MR-SAM can intercept medium-range targets and cooperate in a defensive networked system already at the level of the task group. Finally, the Kusha-derived missile is designed to take care of threats originating at a distance of up to 250 km and beyond, in the ballistic range.
The objective is to create a battle group in which the incoming missile can always be intercepted by the most appropriate weapon, the one that first acquired the target, with the best possible information from ship-based radars, airborne early warning helicopters, and the Integrated Air Command and Control System.

articles.title: AI broke the cybersecurity world. What’s next?
articles.text:
Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now.

This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life.

I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new.

That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era.

There’s a lot going on here — we even got all the way to how AI-powered misinformation and slop might be managed on our social networks.

Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. Welcome back to Decoder.

Hey, thanks for having me, man.

I’m excited to talk to you. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. I feel like you and I talked a lot about how all that was working, about election security, all those sorts of things. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You’ve been thinking about this stuff a lot. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Just give me the lay of land right now.

October is traditionally security awareness month. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached.

You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry.

A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November.

I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? Is it Russia? Is it North Korea? Do we know?

It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up. In cyber, the kill chain is the things you do to have an effect on a target. So to steal information, to turn something off, to steal money, to steal Bitcoin.

Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. And then you have a human being go and take that stuff you built and deploy it against either one target — because maybe you’re a government and you’re going against Lockheed Martin or you’re going against another government or you’re a ransomware actor — and you take all that work you did and you deploy it against hundreds or thousands of targets really fast. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. One of the things that’s happening is that these systems are going and they’re so good at finding bugs that they are finding the bugs in real time and writing the exploits in real time.

The system that everybody’s talking about is not the only one, but the system we’re talking about is a thing called ARTEX, which is a Chinese open-source tool that anybody can go look at. There’s an English translation on GitHub that you can check out. And if you power it on the back end by something like an obliterated GLM-5.3, it will let you break into a shocking number of organizations. This started with three South Korean banks. This week, about 200 more companies have been hit. I’ve been helping a couple of companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It is shocking the companies that are getting hit by something you could just download. It has been a long time since you’ve been able to go and just download an open-source tool and break into multi-billion dollar companies. It’s like the ‘90s. That’s-

That’s what I was thinking about. I think about Windows in the late ’90s, early 2000s when it was a security disaster.

I started saying this actually in the beginning of this year, that it’s an incredibly exciting and terrifying time, because the last time it felt like this was when I was a much younger man and I would go to the very early DEFCONs. DEFCON these days is like 40,000–60,000 people. Back then [in the 1990s] it was a couple hundred people and it was one track and you’d go in and somebody would give a talk and you’d leave the room and you’d think, “Every company in the world is vulnerable to this attack.” The difference was that the entire world didn’t run on the internet. You could go do bad things, but you couldn’t ruin the world and you certainly couldn’t automate it in the way you can now.

It’s back to those days where tools you could just get and build yourself could do crazy things. It’s back to the Wild West days. Back in those days, there were a couple hundred people who had those skills and we were all in one room in Las Vegas and most of them were actually good guys. They didn’t want to be criminals. And now you have a much larger ecosystem of people, many of whom live in places where the law enforcement can’t touch and who have a big economic incentive and have access to these tools. The other big thing is they no longer have to use frontier models that have protections, that have logs that are available to law enforcement. My M5 Mac Ultra Studio finally showed up and I’ve been running a quantized obliterated GLM-5.3 and oh my God, what you can do is incredible.

You mentioned the economics of frontier models. The economy of cyber is one of those things that has gotten sophisticated over the years. One of the things that our systems got safer is you could pay the number of people at DEF CON a whole bunch of money to protect all the systems and it was economically smart to pay them to be defenders instead of attackers. I’m just rewinding my own brain through this history. There was a long conversation in our industry about security through obscurity by hiding all the bugs and hiding all the code versus open source and being really transparent. There was an etiquette that developed about how to reveal the bugs and when to give people notification. There were transparency reports and bug bounties.

You could call it an etiquette, you could call it an economy. We built a culture around cybersecurity and cyber defense and how the attackers and defenders would operate. What you are describing changes it all for a whole number of reasons, but the one that sticks out to me is the economics of it. I can go buy a Mac Studio, I can get an open-weight model and I can just start and that does not place me inside of the culture. There’s not going to be some old man, an Obi-Wan Kenobi saying, “Here’s how you act like a cybersecurity Jedi.” I’m just going to start doing stuff. Tell me how that’s changing right now.

Effectively, the last era of security from my perspective started with the Microsoft, the Bill Gates “trustworthy computing” memo in the early 2000s. And that is when we started designing how we do software security and these big companies, Microsoft and Oracle and then later Amazon and Salesforce and these folks, started hiring ex-hackers. I was part of that generation of the ex-hackers who were at DEF CON and Black Hat and got hired by the companies to go break their stuff. We need to initiate everyone into a way of thinking where the cost of prevention is worth it, and not just the cost of the cure.” Do you think that it’s likely that we’ll slow down? Do you think that we should?

If I had my druthers, I would be fine slowing down on the frontier, and then catching up on the cheaper models for defense. I’m a defense guy. I have to live in the world that other people who work six blocks from me, and who are way, way, way, way richer, make. I live in their world, man. I get asked this question all the time, and I just do the best I can within the world other people make.

Do you think that the big labs have woken up? You mentioned that their cybersecurity teams have gotten more access, and they’ve stopped what you might call the Hugging Face era, or at least they’ve changed the structures of those companies. Do you think that will help?

Certainly they’ve woken up on the eval risk. They have teams, who have been this entire time working very hard on the big picture cyber risk.

Certainly, there are a bunch of people in these companies, as you know, who want to slow down. A lot of that discussion is driven by the P(doom)ers who [are worried] about AI killing us. And that’s never been my concern. Right? And to me, that has always been driven by 24 year olds who all they’ve done is AI and they’ve never done anything else. You and I are both, I think, old enough to remember, I grew up a couple miles from a SAC base and we did drills where I was taught that hiding beneath my public school desk would save me from a Soviet thermonuclear bomb. That was P(doom). My grandfather built a bomb shelter that my mom was taught to hide in during the Cuban Missile Crisis. That was P(doom). There’s a youth issue and a never-doing-anything-but-AI issue of people who they got their undergraduate, their master’s, and their PhD only doing linear algebra and neural networks and never touching anything else.

I have always been much more concerned about the human uplift risk from AI, of all the risks about human beings using AI to do bad things to other human beings. Part of my concern is that there has been success in these labs working together on not letting LLMs encrypt their chain of thought. Because when they talk about pacing the frontier, it’s for the P(doom) stuff, for the polycules that live together in Berkeley. They’re talking about very specific stuff about keeping control of the models themselves, which I think is great. That stuff needs to happen. But if those things happen, then there’s still often an increase in a bunch of capabilities that human beings can use.

I really prefer there to be a broader discussion on whether we could make these things less human-seeming. I don’t think these things should have personality. I think the goal of these things should be to serve humans. They should not seem to have souls. They should not seem to have personality. I think for a lot of the negative impacts — as somebody who was at Facebook and saw what it was like for that company to have negative impacts on people — there should be a much broader feeling at these companies of what are we doing broadly to people. A lot of that could just be, “Don’t have these things ever act like somebody’s friend.” At a maximum, it should act like… Like the people, I don’t know what the company is, but the people who made the, “Hi, I’m a really nice…” Like the photorealistic girl who will chat with you, that is to me spectacularly unethical to even try that, to even start that. That’s the kind of thing that we should just make. I don’t know if we can make it illegal, but we should make it completely societally not acceptable to work on that kind of stuff. Right?

That’s a great segue because I did want to ask you about Facebook and content moderation. Like I said, you and I first started talking a long time ago about content moderation in the context of security. You would get foreign nation states flooding our algorithms with all kinds of misinformation during elections, and that was a security problem.

I open Instagram today and I am confronted with some of the most nightmare copyright law hypotheticals to have ever existed in the history of the world. The one I got today was a deep fake of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc doing “Somebody That I Used to Know.” And I thought, “50 different people can probably sue Meta right now.” This is hilarious if you know what happened in that last race.

So we keep talking about it. We’ve posted some clips of us talking about it on The Vergecast where I said, “I think Meta is letting their AI ambitions crush Instagram.” Instagram is being flooded with slop in a very particular way. Some people love it, sometimes it’s funny, but there’s a nightmare set of lawsuits coming. There’s a whole rights management problem coming. The users don’t like it and they should label it. They should label it and let you filter it.

So we posted this and Adam Mosseri said this to us in a reply on Threads, “I would love to do this. I’m worried that the models are going to get ahead of us, that we can try to do this, but there’s not actually a way to recognize AI content. There’s not actually a way to label it well. If you’re worried about the sexy AI influencers stealing jokes from a comedian, now you got to build a database of jokes.” You have some history here. I think Instagram is about to go through it in a real way. Is there some technical solution to the problem of AI slop in social media?

Mosseri is right that it’s not perfect, but also something I noticed during my time at Facebook was that when Facebook doesn’t want to do something, they will allow the technical challenges to stop them. When Facebook really wants to do something, they will give it their all. That is the pattern always.

When I wanted to try really hard on the safety issue, man, this is not solvable. You’re right, it’s never perfectly solvable, but let’s give it a shot. But whenever Mark Zuckerberg is told something is impossible — it’s impossible to monetize mobile, it’s impossible to build this network to two billion people, it’s going to be impossible to monetize WhatsApp, it’s going to be impossible to work AI into the system while maintaining data encryption — he’s been told that everything’s impossible over and over again and then he constantly succeeds. They will give it a shot and they will do it. But when they don’t want to do something, oh, that’s impossible.

Do you think that there’s some way to understand that some piece of media is generated by AI in a consistent and verifiable way? This to me seems like the challenge.

I am not as up on the literature here. Up to this point, there has been a pretty decent arms race. By definition, AI will continue to get better because — especially for visual models, for diffusion models — the way they work is that you have detection oracles that they test against. Certainly, you can never have something open source because it will immediately end up in the diffusion model. But for closed-source oracles where then you do not make it easy for them to test the oracle, one of the key things you do in trust and safety is then you have delayed enforcement mechanisms so they can’t brute force and test. I think it is quite possible.

Let’s say I was still at Meta. My advice to them would be to also explore a variety of different detection mechanisms outside of the content itself. I would do the best I can on the content, but I would also be doing as low level access as possible to the camera. I would only let content come from the camera.

And what I would say is, Nilay’s completely correct, there’s a massive hunger for, especially among young people, stuff that is authentic. I have three teenagers and they hate AI. They hate AI slop. They have a massive negative reaction. My wife and I created just a cute little family AI thing and they yell at us about a bunch of stuff, but they lost their minds about this cute little family AI thing because they just hate it.

So I think somebody is going to come and disrupt Instagram and it’s going to be because… There’s already, I’ve seen these little things where it’s like you take the photo during the day, be real and stuff. There’s these little things, but somebody’s going to massively disrupt Instagram because they’re taking the images of the photos straight off the camera and then all the editing is going to be only within the app and they’re going to do things to make sure that nothing can make it into the pipeline from AI. You’re going to allow some kind of CapCut-like functionality that never has an AI component. I think that is going to be a killer app.

Man, I could do another whole hour with you on this because the system you’re describing there is not detecting AI content, it is verifying real content.

It’s much easier. Verifying real content is much easier. And there’s been a big focus on this on the professional side, like Adobe has a whole thing where if you’re a New York Times photographer, you have a $5,000 Nikon or Canon camera, you take the photo and it’s cryptographically verified.

Yeah, but the iPhone that I’m holding here has that in it now. Right? Like there’s a lot of —

Right, the iPhone has it now.

Yeah. There’s a lot of this out there, but it’s the other side that I’m thinking about where it’s “We are going to detect AI text.” The leading model companies because of European regulations are now futzing with the text they generate.

Text is much harder because you just have so much less data. Especially in 140 characters, what do you have in there to detect? The more you’ve got, the more you can do.

It is amazing because I can detect Claude a mile away. So maybe I’ll just rely on my own human ability.

Yeah, but not in tweet length.

That’s true. The cheap ones, I can. But I’m just saying the notion that we’re going to verify what’s real instead of detecting what’s fake feels very important in the context of the media we consume.

Detecting what’s fake is always going to be probabilistic and we’re going to asymptotically approach impossibility, whereas detecting what’s real can be cryptographically perfect. I would not pick the battle that we will eventually lose. I would pick the battle that we can cryptographically win. That would be my suggestion.

And there’s somewhere in there where you have to build an entire chain of custody. We’re going to take the sensor data off the camera. We’re going to put it in a cloud server. We’re only going to allow edits on this server. That file will never get monkeyed with.

Sure, that’s true for the New York Times and Adobe Photoshop and stuff, but not for Instagram. For Instagram, you can do it all because it’s only the iPhone and it’s only Instagram. So the entire chain of custody is within your app, it is within the iPhone sensor and it’s in Instagram. So it’s actually easy for them.

Yeah. Look, like I said, We could do another whole hour on that because it feels like right next to the cybersecurity problem is the social engineering problem, and right next to the social engineering problem is the fake media problem.

No, absolutely.

How many phishing attacks are just “this website looked pretty real”?

Oh, yeah.

Or this person is talking to you or there’s an AI voice on the other side of the phone. And all of that comes down to whether you can detect what’s fake instead of verifying what’s real? And I don’t know the answer.

Oh, no. I’ve had to train my parents that, “If you get a video from your grandchildren saying they’ve been kidnapped, you have to call me because the odds that it’s real are not very high.” That’s where we’re at as a society.

I feel like I want to end on a hopeful note and I don’t know how to do it from there.

Wrong guest for that, buddy.

This is why you only come on every few years. Now after this, we’re going to do the series of birthday party guests. You’ve been talking about the dark ages. We’re in it, where it’s starting to accelerate. What are the markers people should look for in terms of progress to say, “Okay, we’re climbing our way back up”?

AI is great for lots of things. I think AI is going to enable individuals. We’re going to see a huge explosion of new companies. Stanford students have always been entrepreneurial, but the number of my students who are now starting two-, three-, four-person companies who are doing incredible things, who used to need to hire 50 or 100 people and take a ton of venture capital, is incredible. We’re going to continue to see that.

One of the things we hopefully see is a downtick in the number of major breaches at some point. We should hopefully see a downtick in the major CVEs that are wormable and that are in the fundamental infrastructure pieces kernel wheel. Like I said, I want Linux to be rewritten, but hopefully we see a downtick in the Linux kernel and those other kinds of libraries, openSSL, glibc, things like that.

Maybe I should vibe code this up, but I think it would be cool to have an index of where we are in the cycle, of like an artificial index of all of these, the Dow for all of the libraries of where we’re going. Plus right now, Patch Tuesday used to be like 150, 200, got to 300, 600. I think the last one was 900 something, so we’re geometrically growing. It’d be nice to see Patch Tuesday start to go back down. Apple patches are the same thing. Yep, you inspired me. I’m going to create a Dow index for this, the dark age index. And then maybe we can publish it on The Verge.

Yeah, that’d be great.

But I think these are the kinds of things that it would be nice to see a reversal for. What would be especially nice to see is that the day or actually like 30 days before you get the next version of OpenAI and Anthropic cyber models, that you don’t have this huge round of patches because what’s happening is those guys are running their models against Microsoft’s code, against a bunch of open source, and they’re giving all the bugs away and you don’t know where the bugs are coming from. It’s just like anonymous reports for 1,000 bugs in the Linux kernel. And then a month later, here’s the new Astra Cyber. So if those get smaller and smaller every time, then it means that we’re starting to reach some kind of steady state.

You should definitely do that tracker. We will definitely publish it. Alex, it has been incredible to have you on the show. We’ll have to talk again soon.

Yeah, thank you so much. I think you do some of the best journalism on this stuff and I really appreciate it.

articles.title: Fireworks says you’re wasting money on AI unless you’re using all the models
articles.text:
Fireworks AI is fine with helping companies run AI models in their own datacenters, though VP Rob Ferguson argues against doing so.

Ferguson told The Register in an interview that while Fireworks AI, a managed inference provider, supports on-prem AI, "we're trying to push people more and more away from it because frankly, it's just the economics."

The GPU hardware is just so expensive that if you can't keep it fully utilized, it's a waste of money, he contends. Ten thousand GPUs, he said, represent a billion dollars of capital.

"You don't want those things to be sitting idle," he said.

For companies with particularly sensitive workloads, Ferguson said, Fireworks is happy to work something out – it offers a service called Sovereign for just that purpose and it has partners like Microsoft that can help. But most inference work probably doesn't need that level of protection, he said.

"The state of the art for everyone is to have a portfolio of models," he explained. "In fact, I think most people don't know that the best model in the world's not Astra. The best model in the world's not Fable. The best model is literally a portfolio and we can prove it. You are always better routing between a few models than to do one singular model."

That's what Fireworks does through Nexus and its API, alongside competitors like Together AI, Baseten, and DeepInfra. As a managed inference platform, Fireworks AI routes inference tasks to whichever model, frontier model subscription, or API is best suited to handle them.

But the company is not just doing naive routing like an AI gateway. It's evaluating tasks as they come in and directing them to the optimal model.

"We build custom routers," Ferguson explained. "Our auto model is continuously updating so that we actually go through and we grade the difficulty of the task and we see if there're affinities that the models have, like Kimi is slightly better at JavaScript than Python, things like this."

The company's competitive edge, he contends, is its crack engineering team, which follows from its founders' work on PyTorch, a widely used open source machine learning library.

"We're performance experts both on the training and inference side," he explained. "People I think don't understand how important, for example, numerics is. So when you use a model, it's always called a mixture of experts – an expert is a different machine.

"And so you have all these different machines. It actually matters when you're training that you go back to precisely the right machine, because if you don't, the other machine will still answer the question, but it'll answer in a slightly different way. So we have to know how to build the topology to write back the data to the right space. We have to understand floating point precision [to handle very small values]. We have to be able to do all this where we're routing through a complex fabric through potentially more than one provider depending on what everything is. And so we're really systems experts."

Hyperscalers, he argues, will give you a GPU but then it's your responsibility to put it to use. Fireworks' advantage involves being able to maximize utilization at scale while maintaining model precision and speed.

Ferguson said AI keeps coming back to economics.

"People are just trying to figure out more and more things to use AI for and [to answer questions like] just how much more can I send to cached models, how much more can I send to open models, when do I need this specialization?" he said. "So we're constantly working with customers to help them come up with their own evaluation criteria."

One reason for this, Ferguson explained, is that frontier model companies are not transparent about their caching rates. He said Fireworks was working with a data science company and was caching about 90 percent of the tasks.

"We looked at [Anthropic's] Opus and it was caching 30 percent of the time," he said. "It was doing AI rework constantly. And with AI, rework is by far your biggest cost. If it's not hitting a cache, then your costs are absolutely insane. And so the token cost is not the real cost. It's the cost per task. And they're hiding that from you. And so we always tell our customers to be tracking cost per task, because that's the real number."

Another factor that companies should consider in their cost calculations, Ferguson suggested, is the value of their data and whether they're giving that data away for training.

"I think people grossly underestimate the value of their data," he said.

Fireworks AI has a zero data-retention policy, "but a lot of times," Ferguson said, "these other companies [do] not, and you should be getting paid for your data. Nobody really knew at the beginning of this current era that these models are memorizers. But now there's plenty of evidence that these models are. So if they're going to be using your data, then you should be getting value for it."

But it's not just about cost. Speed, said Ferguson, is underappreciated.

"Speed is the thing that people often don't know they can ask for," he said. "It's such a game changer for me and how I work with AI is so different when the responses come back as fast as I ask them."

What's the advantage of model ensembling, as the company refers to its model routing activities? A bill that's at least 50 percent smaller, Ferguson claims.

"So we say six to eight times cheaper," he said. "The reality is that because a lot of folks have a preference in their tooling, we kinda guarantee that in the case where you're still using a combo of closed and open models, we can always guarantee that your bill will drop by half right away. Like we're sure about that. And then the question is can we just get you to use more stuff?" ®

articles.title: India Develops Ultra-Sensitive Atomic Magnetometer for Defence
articles.text:
India is looking to develop atomic magnetometers through a collaboration between the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) in Hyderabad. This could help future defence, navigation, geological and other high-precision sensing applications.
A team of researchers at TIFR Hyderabad are working with DRDO’s Young Scientist Laboratory for Quantum Technologies (DYSL-QT). One of the main goals of the collaborative project, advertised on the TIFR Hyderabad website, is to develop a magnetometer sensor package for an atomic magnetometer with high sensitivity to femto-Tesla levels.
As shown in the attached image, the project aims to scale up from an initial proof of concept pico-Tesla sensitivity magnetometer to a smaller sensor package and field testing. The project will be conducted in collaboration with TIFR Hyderabad and aims to improve the magnetometer sensitivity to femto-Tesla levels.
Unlike traditional magnetometers, atomic magnetometers measure very small magnetic fields by interacting light with atomic systems. TIFR Hyderabad explain how they work by stating they “utilise the interaction between resonant light and alkali atoms. Any change in the spin optical response of the alkali atoms can be used to determine the magnetic field”.
These extremely sensitive magnetometers can help defence applications by navigating in situations where traditional satellite navigation may not be available. By mapping magnetic fields you can gain insight into your surrounding environment which can lead to new navigation systems.
The technology could also be used for geological sensing. TIFR Hyderabad currently have research into developing atomic magnetometers and quantum sensing platforms for navigation, defence and geological applications. They have developed portable systems with pico-Tesla sensitivity.
This project is particularly important due to where it is heading. In the previous collaborative project between DRDO and TIFR, the researchers have already demonstrated pico-Tesla sensitivity at room temperature over a frequency range of ~1–50 kHz. The goal of this is to improve the sensitivity to femto-Tesla levels and develop a DC-cum-AC magnetometer for geological applications.
This confirms that this is part of the wider Quantum Technologies that DRDO have been working on. The Quantum Technologies project states they are working on the development of an Atomic Vapor Magnetometer and magnetometer sensor package for atomic magnetometers with high sensitivity to femto-Tesla levels.
This is also becoming more than just a research project. Recently TIFR Hyderabad have stated they are working towards an atomic magnetometer that can be deployed in the field. Their research project aims to increase the sensitivity to magnetic fields.
This is an important aspect of the project. If the magnetometer is not small enough to be deployed in the field then there is little point having a highly sensitive magnetometer. The true breakthrough would be having a highly sensitive magnetometer that is small and stable enough to be deployed on a vehicle, aircraft, vessel etc.
There is potential for this to help with navigation. The magnetometer could be used to compliment inertial navigation and satellite positioning in the future. However, this should not be viewed as a quick replacement for current navigation systems. There would be a lot of development and testing needed in the field.
Overall this project is not just another magnetometer but is part of India’s efforts to develop homegrown quantum sensing technologies. This could eventually allow us to have sovereign solutions in areas where we traditionally rely on highly specialised foreign technologies.

Kalyani Strategic Systems Bids for Greek Ammunition Plant
articles.text:
India’s Kalyani Strategic Systems Limited (KSSL), part of the Kalyani Group, will compete against Germany’s Rheinmetall to win a contract to modernise and manage a large ammunition manufacturing plant in Greece – another step in expanding India’s private defence sector in Europe.
KSSL has submitted an expression of interest to bid in the international tender alongside one of Greece’s largest infrastructure and construction firms, GEK TERNA. The competitor bid comes from Rheinmetall Waffe Munition GmbH, a subsidiary of Germany’s Rheinmetall Group.
The tender relates to the modernisation and management of EAS’ industrial facilities in Aigio in the Achaea region of Greece. It includes the funding, modernisation and management of large calibre ammunition shell and cartridge cases.
The tender will see the winning consortium be responsible for the funding and modernisation of the current machinery and industrial facilities at the EAS plant. They will also gain rights and responsibility to manage and develop the manufacturing operations.
The tender is significant due to the increase in demand for artillery ammunition and military supplies in Europe meaning they want to boost their manufacturing.
The Aigio plant could be a key manufacturing site for large calibre ammunition, as the European governments want to boost local manufacturing.
This is a great opportunity for Kalyani Strategic Systems to enter the European market with its well-established ammunition manufacturing capabilities. This tender is notable as Rheinmetall are one of Europe’s leading defence manufacturers.
The involvement of the German firm means there is a strong manufacturing element involved in the tender. KSSL are partnering with GEK TERNA meaning they have manufacturing experience from the Indian defence sector.
The set up could give Kalyani access to European manufacturing capabilities and potentially opportunities within the regional area, depending on what the conditions of the concession are.
Kalyani Group have been increasing their defence manufacturing capabilities through Bharat Forge and its defence focused subsidiaries. They manufacture artillery, ammunition, armour and more. The expressions of interest are the first stage of the international tender. EAS will assess the bids and prequalify the interested parties.
The next stage will be a competitive dialogue between the shortlisted companies and the Greek company. Once this is complete they will issue binding offers and choose the winning concessionaire.

articles.title: Emergency a mistake: Sonia Gandhi
articles.text: New Delhi: Weighing in on the Emergency, Congress leader Sonia Gandhi has called the decision to impose it a mistake and said that she believes that her mother-in-law and then prime minister Indira Gandhi also came to feel the same.The Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson in her upcoming book "Belonging: A Journey of Love" also writes that keeping Sanjay Gandhi "in check" could have prevented much of the damage that followed the imposition of the Emergency, according to The Guardian.Also Read: Sonia Gandhi says Penguin was 'uneasy' with criticism of govtIn an interview with the British daily ahead of the launch of her memoir, Sonia Gandhi said, "I always feel that Mrs (Indira) Gandhi was a democrat at heart.""I know that many would laugh at this, but I believe she was never comfortable in the course of the emergency. I think it was sitting heavy on her," she added.Sonia Gandhi, who also holds the distinction of being the longest serving president of the Congress, was quoted by the British daily as saying that it was a mistake for Indira Gandhi to call the Emergency, and that she believes her mother-in-law came to feel the same.Also Read: 'I will carry national flag across country, even if arrested': CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke at Kochi protestAccording to Gandhi, the family was split on the decision of Emergency.Sonia Gandhi's husband Rajiv was against the move, telling his mother to wait for the next election, but her younger son Sanjay pushed for it, arguing at one family dinner that the opposition would destroy his mother and telling her, "They must be stopped", the Guardian reported.Sonia Gandhi was quoted as saying that it inflamed tensions within the family, too, as Rajiv attempted to confront his mother, but she refused to listen."Keeping Sanjay in check could have prevented much of the damage that followed," Gandhi writes in her book, according to The Guardian.In another interview published in The Hindu on Saturday ahead of the launch of her book, Gandhi has also spoken about the turbulent times of the Emergency.She said that hindsight allows people to put things better in perspective and pointed out that Indira Gandhi herself later publicly expressed regret and apologised for excesses during the Emergency.Asked about Sanjay Gandhi's name becoming synonymous with the Emergency, and whether the excesses of that time could have been avoided had Indira Gandhi listened to her elder son Rajiv and to others, Sonia Gandhi said, "It was not only Sanjay, though in the public mind he is often seen as synonymous with the Emergency. There was a lot of pressure from some of her senior colleagues, and I think there were very few people around her like Rajiv who had a different point of view.""I think eventually my mother-in-law began to understand the situation through her own wisdom and took actions to remedy it," she said."It was only after the Emergency that I came to know the true gravity of what had been happening. There was a laissez-faire kind of an attitude," she said.Emergency was imposed by Indira Gandhi just before midnight of June 25, 1975. President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed issued the proclamation at Gandhi's behest that was later ratified by the Union Cabinet.On January 18, 1977, Indira Gandhi called for fresh elections and released all political prisoners.On March 16, 1977, Indira Gandhi and son Sanjay were defeated in Lok Sabha elections and on March 21 that year, the Emergency officially came to an end.The BJP has been criticising the Congress over the Emergency, calling it a "murder of democracy".The Modi government has been observing 'Samvidhan Hatya Diwas' to mark the "dark phase" in Indian democracy.

articles.text:
While there has been genuine interest from the Indian Navy for the F-35B Lightning II from the United States, Lockheed Martin has also looked at supplying the aircraft to India, however it has never been incorporated into any funded procurement programmes.
Some confusion stems from the fact that in 2020, India signed an inter-governmental agreement for 26 Rafale-M carrier fighters to be supplied at a cost of around 63,000 crore. However, despite US President Donald Trump publicly offering the F-35 to India during this time, New Delhi has not pursued procurement. Therefore there are no orders for any F-35s (B variant or otherwise).
India’s first known public display of interest for the F-35 was on 11th July 2005 when, following the commissioning of INS Beas in Kolkata, then Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Arun Prakash said he preferred the Lockheed Martin F-35 Joint Strike Fighter to the Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet due to compatibility issues with the ski jump.
India’s carriers are designed for STOBAR operations (Short Take-Off But Arrested Recovery), so the F-35B which is designed for Short Take-off and vertical landing, appears to have been a good option to add a 5th generation stealth fighter to India’s fleet with little changes to the launch system.
As far back as 2010, when the Navy were seeking information on a new generation carrier fighter, Lockheed Martin has produced information on the F-35B and F-35C (catapult version). They were also looking at adapting the F-35C to ski jump using simulations and structural analysis. This is purely exploratory though and does not indicate India had chosen or looked at both variants. In 2017 the Navy moved towards a competitive Multi-Role Carrier Borne Fighter (MRCBF) procurement, which included the Rafale M, F/A-18E/F Super Hornet, Gripen Maritime and MiG-29K.
The F-35 wasn’t entered by Lockheed Martin. They indicated that they would not sell the F-35 unless there was a strategic initiative from government. Due to the competitive nature of the procurement, the F-35 was now out of contention.
The Navy’s future direction became clear that it wanted a twin engine carrier fighter with the range, payload and recovery capabilities to operate for long periods of time over the Indian Ocean. This doesn’t fit with the single engined F-35B.
5 Reasons why the F-35B was never purchased:
- No Procurement Programme: Despite public displays of interest and talks with Lockheed Martin there was no procurement programme set up to purchase the F-35B.
- Operational Requirements: The Navy wanted a twin engine fighter to operate from the deck, meaning the indigenous Twin Engine Deck Based Fighter (TEDBF) programme didn’t fit with the single engine F-35B.
- Range & Payload Capabilities: The F-35B suffers from compromises in fuel, payload and bring back due to the lift fan and STOVL design. As the navy will be operating over long distances the F-35B would not be ideal. The ski jump launch can also impact the amount of usable fuel and weapons.
- Sovereignty: India is focusing more on having a domestically designed, manufactured and maintained fleet for their carriers. The Rafale-M deal has stipulations for India to have some industrial and maintenance elements. The F-35 has a highly restricted global support and mission data network, meaning the industrial aspect wouldn’t be the same.
- Cost & Timing: For the F-35B to have been purchased there would have been a separate political decision made in Washington, changes to infrastructure, training, maintenance and integration. It could have also caused complications with the funding and development of the indigenous TEDBF.
The purchase of the S-400 and the risk of being sanctioned under CAATSA has also added some complication to any large deal with the Americans. However, no sanctions have been placed by Washington. The Navy had a quick solution to improve their carrier fleet with the agreement to purchase 26 Rafale-M fighters in 2025. Whilst the F-35B isn’t a stealth aircraft and doesn’t have the vertical landing capabilities, the Rafale M fits within the Navy’s traditional carrier fighter approach. It can also easily integrate into the current Rafale ecosystem in India.

articles.title: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
articles.text:
It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters.

At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors.

Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads.

articles.title: UAV TECH Develops Super-Sonic Twin-Jet MSTARC-200 Aerial Target
articles.text:
Hyderabad-based UAV TECH Private Limited are developing the MSTARC-200 for advanced aerial threat simulation. This system will be used for air defence training, weapon testing and interception. The plane will be a reusable aerial target simulating various signatures.
The MSTARC-200 will have a lightweight composite structure, twin jet propulsion and will have high speed capabilities. The system will be able to perform high G (up to 8G) and will be used to simulate various threat situations.
The MSTARC-200 is recoverable using a parachute instead of being disposable. This will allow the plane to be inspected and repaired allowing it to be reused. This reduces the overall costs of the aerial target. UAV TECH state recovery and repair are an integral part of their sustainable development.
As per the specification the MSTARC-200 has a 2.33m wingspan, length of 3.7m and weighs 240kg. It can carry payloads up to 40kg. The aircraft will have a top speed of 250m/s and a cruise speed of 150m/s. It can operate up to a service ceiling of 10,000m ASL. It can also operate at low altitudes with a minimum altitude of 20m.
The aircraft will be able to simulate various situations. This includes low-level approaches, sea-skimming and high altitude targeting. As per the specification the MSTARC-200 boasts a catapult launch system for fast deployment.
One of the key features of the MSTARC-200 is its modular payload system. The aircraft will have various components to simulate various signatures.
These include hot nose modules, IR flares and smoke flares. The aircraft can also be fitted with chaff dispensers, IFF transponders, radar cross-section enhancement and programmable active radar enhancement. The system can also be fitted with Luneberg lenses to increase the radar cross section. This will allow the aircraft to be more visible on radar. The aircraft also has a radar altimeter and sea-skimming module.
The aircraft will have acoustic and Doppler radar to aid telemetry and analysis. This will allow testing teams to see how well radars and tracking systems can detect and track various targets.
The MSTARC-200 could be used to test surface-to-air missiles, radar systems, electronic warfare and interception. Having an aerial target that can vary the radar and IR signature will allow test agencies to have a more diverse range of engagement scenarios. UAV TECH have not given much detail on how far they have got with flight testing, what type of engines they will be using, how long it can fly for and how long until it is inducted. These factors will be important in determining how capable the aircraft really is.

Brazilian aerospace major Embraer is eyeing setting up India as a production and exporting hub for its C-390 Millennium military transport plane, possibly using Nagpur as an entire production hub, supplying planes built in India to customers in Asia.
“It is very important to us to have India as a strategic partner. articles.title: NHS breach helpline left staff carrying a 'significant emotional burden'
articles.text:
NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review has found.

The report [PDF] comes almost exactly a year after the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust disclosed a data breach affecting 8,003 people, including current and former trust staff and non-trust workers.

A member of the public discovered the exposure in November 2025. An Excel workbook published in response to a Freedom of Information request in February 2023 retained underlying sickness absence records that users could reveal through its pivot tables.

Staff assigned to the helpline described difficult calls involving shouting, anger, and distress.

Particularly difficult calls involved people distressed by the sensitivity of the disclosures or potentially in danger from domestic abuse. Call handlers said they had to make safeguarding assessments without training or an established process.

"Such occurrences of anger or distress were not infrequent, and this reflected the heightened emotions and distress experienced by callers to varying degrees due to the breach," the review noted.

"This placed significant emotional burden on individuals working in the contact center, who were not prepared or provided support on how to deal with those."

Members of the trust's clinical governance team were told just a day beforehand that they would staff the helpline. Despite their experience dealing with patient trauma, they received little preparation for the calls that followed.

"The staff working in the call centers had a short training session and then the calls started coming in within minutes of the team being set up," the review noted. "Some staff had not finished reading the pre-prepared script which had arrived only 30 minutes before the center went live."

Most call handlers only learned that their own data had been exposed while already working on the helpline, sometimes minutes before supporting others affected.

Call handlers also said they had little choice about taking on the work and were expected to maintain their usual duties alongside it.

The review stated that some staff members gave up weekends and worked long past their scheduled hours to meet the demands of both roles.

"It's typical NHS, it runs on goodwill," one staffer told the team that compiled the report.

The call center was only supposed to run for two weeks in December 2025, but due to the volume of calls, it was eventually stood down after 11 weeks, in February 2026.

According to officials speaking at a trust board meeting on Thursday, the review and its findings have since been circulated among staff, and published online.

How the spreadsheet slipped through

Responding to a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request thought to be from a journalist researching a story about stress in the NHS, the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust uploaded a spreadsheet to its public FOI Disclosure log in February 2023.

This contained personal data and inadvertently exposed sickness absence information and sensitive health data related to 7,715 staff, 288 non-trust workers, as well as a small number of unidentified records.

Crucially, this spreadsheet was uploaded in a format that allowed users to access the pivot table from which some data was derived. The data in these pivot tables would normally have been too sensitive to be included in FOIA responses.

The first failure was that the request was handled by the trust's e-Rostering team instead of the People Information Unit, which had the expertise in responding to FOIA requests with complex datasets.

The e-Rostering team compiled the response using the team's own data, but incorrectly believed they had stripped the spreadsheet of the sensitive data that would later be exposed.

Standard procedures instructed request handlers to follow several steps to ensure sensitive data was stripped before documents are published, some of which were skipped.

For starters, one FOI officer assigned to the response either failed to run the spreadsheet through Excel's Document Inspector, which formed part of the usual procedures, or failed to act upon its recommendations.

This feature can flag pivot tables and potentially hidden cached data, but cannot determine whether that data is sensitive or automatically remove the cache.

Staff also failed to follow instructions to convert the spreadsheet to PDF. Investigators found that doing so prevented users clicking through to the underlying records, although they could not guarantee that no hidden data remained technically accessible.

At the time, internal guidance did not require conversion to CSV, which would have removed the workbook's pivot-table functionality and embedded cache.

The trust's sign-off process also focused on answering the request's questions and meeting their public relations duties, and falsely assumed that the data had been adequately sanitized before the final review.

The spreadsheet was made available for 33 months, although the trust is not sure how many times it was viewed during that time.

Its logs only covered the 12 months before a member of the public alerted it to the pivot table issue. These indicated that it had been accessed 340 times, although the review noted there was no way of knowing how many of these, if any, led to pivot tables being accessed, or even if it was viewed by a human, with web crawlers adding to the total view count.

The trust has since implemented a number of changes to prevent a recurrence of the breach, including the mandatory password-protecting of any Excel workbook as part of FOIA responses.

A senior information governance officer must now approve spreadsheet responses before executive sign-off. Revised guidance circulated in November 2025 also called for conversion to CSV, although investigators found that this requirement had not been incorporated into the formal operating procedure and recommended updating it.

The review says the Information Commissioner's Office closed its case after the trust implemented its recommendations.

A spokesperson for the Royal Cornwall Hospitals said: "We are deeply sorry for the accidental sharing of sickness absence data which we reported in November 2025, and for the distress and concern it caused those colleagues whose data was involved.

"An independent investigation has now been completed, and the report has been published in full on our website in the interests of transparency and accountability.

"The investigation has helped us understand what happened and identify areas where improvements were needed. We have already implemented a number of measures to strengthen our processes, particularly around the management of Freedom of Information requests and responses.

"The protection of personal information is of the utmost importance to us, and we remain committed to learning from this incident and preventing a similar event from happening again.

"We continue to provide support to colleagues who have been affected." ®

articles.title: Windows takes a break at UK motorway services
articles.text:
A roadside display at Cherwell Valley services has stopped dispensing information and started asking for help.

The eagle-eyed Register reader who spotted the stricken screen told us: "UK motorway signs often tell us that tiredness can kill, urging us to take a break. This poor thing at Cherwell Valley services took the advice to heart."

The display at the Moto services appears to have run into trouble during a restart. Windows offers another attempt or access to repair tools, although the latter options are hidden – perhaps somewhere on the top floor of the neighboring Travelodge. Getting things moving again will probably require access to the computer behind the screen.

The Automatic Repair screen is all too familiar to Windows users. Not to be confused with the classic blue screen of death, it might indicate a misbehaving driver during a reboot, an update that did something unexpected, or some sort of hardware failure. Hopefully it isn't the latter – with memory and storage prices the way they are at the moment, a motorway services sandwich or gallon of fuel will seem a positive bargain by comparison.

Our reader is right: taking a break is sensible advice. Getting Windows to end one can be another matter. ®
